archetype.name: Playoff Team (pass-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose record matches its play. A top-five passing offense carries it, and a middling defense, a broken run game and a pile of giveaways keep it from looking like last year's juggernaut.

report.headline: A top-five passing attack giving the ball away is why this is 4-3
report.take:
Last year's Patriots went 14-3 with the league's best offense by EPA. This version is built the same way and simply less efficient. Drake Maye has started every game and the pass offense ranks 5th in EPA per play (0.218), but it now carries everything. The run game is 28th in rush EPA, and the defense sits at 16th in EPA allowed, right in the middle. Net EPA is 11th and the point differential is 10th. A winsOverExpected of 0.5 says the 4-3 record is about what this team has earned. That is a contrast with 2025, when the same number ranked 2nd and flattered the 14 wins.

The defining number is the turnover margin. New England is 31st in turnover differential per game at -1, with 14 giveaways against 7 takeaways. That explains how an offense 7th in yards per game is only 19th in points per game: drives that move the ball keep ending without points. The early season was the worst of it. The losses to Seattle and Jacksonville came with three turnovers each and passing EPA of -4.6 and -13.9. Since the Buffalo upset, the pass game has been strongly positive every week, and the giveaways have come down to one or two a game.

The numbers flatter the run game less than the yardage suggests. The backs average 2.7 yards before contact, 10th in the league, so the line is creating some room. But 3.67 yards a carry and a 28th-ranked run success rate mean little happens after contact. A 148-yard rushing day against the Jets still graded at -7 rush EPA. On defense, a 9th-ranked points-allowed figure hides real leaks in the secondary: 23rd in explosive pass rate and 23rd in deep-pass EPA allowed, with 308 passing yards given up in Chicago.

The road ahead is harder in the trenches and on the back end. Starting guard Alijah Vera-Tucker is on IR, center Ben Brown is out, and Carlton Davis III, a 95%-snap corner, is out with a neck injury. That hits a line already 26th in pressure rate allowed, protecting a quarterback who holds the ball 3.11 seconds, 2nd-longest. After Miami, the schedule turns brutal: Buffalo, Minnesota, Kansas City, Denver and a Detroit offense ranked 3rd. This looks like a playoff team if the turnover rate keeps normalizing, and a wild-card bubble team if it doesn't.

strengths.title: Maye's passing game drives everything
strengths.body: The pass offense ranks 5th in EPA per play and has been strongly positive in every game since Week 4, peaking at 29.5 passing EPA against Las Vegas. This is a continuation of 2025's top-ranked offense rather than a fluke, so it should hold. The risk is the protection behind it, not the quarterback.

strengths.title: Moves the ball and sustains drives
strengths.body: An offense 7th in yards per game, holding the ball over 30 minutes a game, with an 11th-ranked success rate keeps a mid-tier defense off the field. Paired with Vrabel going for it on every fourth-down opportunity that qualifies (1st in go rate), the Patriots squeeze extra possessions' worth of value out of long drives.

strengths.title: Defense limits points better than plays
strengths.body: The defense is only 16th in EPA allowed, but 9th in points allowed thanks to a 10th-ranked third-down rate and a pass rush with 17 sacks. The bend-don't-break profile is real but thin. It relies on third-down stops more than down-to-down quality, and that kind of edge tends to drift toward average.

concerns.title: Giveaways are wasting a good offense
concerns.body: Fourteen turnovers in seven games and a -7 margin is the gap between 19th in scoring and 7th in yardage. Some of it is the early-season slump, and turnover margin is noisy, so expect improvement. But a quarterback holding the ball 3.11 seconds behind a leaky line will keep putting the ball at risk.

concerns.title: Protection breaking down, now short-handed
concerns.body: The line is 26th in pressure rate allowed already. It has now lost Vera-Tucker to IR and Ben Brown to a knee injury. Maye's long time to throw raises his ceiling downfield but makes him dependent on the interior holding up, which is exactly where the injuries are.

concerns.title: Run game adds nothing
concerns.body: Rush EPA of -0.2 (27th) and a 33.9% run success rate mean the ground game is a drain even when the yardage looks fine. The line gives 2.7 yards before contact, so the shortfall is after contact, with the backs. That makes it a personnel problem that won't fix itself. With center and guard down, it could get worse.

trend.note: The passing EPA was negative in each of the first three games and strongly positive in all four since, with turnovers easing to one or two a game. The defense, though, has given up more passing yardage in recent weeks, capped by 308 in Chicago.

nextGame.headline: Miami's worst-in-league pass defense meets a surging Maye
nextGame.body:
New England travels to Miami as a 7.5-point favorite (moneyline -395, total 44.5) with ten days of rest after the Thursday game in Chicago. The matchup lines up cleanly for the Patriots' strength. Miami ranks 32nd in defensive pass EPA, 30th in pressure rate with only 6 sacks, 31st in third-down rate allowed, and 30th in deep-pass EPA allowed. Miami's offense under Malik Willis wants to run instead, at a pass rate over expected that ranks 31st, behind a line that leads the league in yards before contact. That is the one place it can test a New England run defense that ranks 25th in rushing yards allowed.

Availability tilts both ways. The Patriots are without CB Carlton Davis III, C Ben Brown and G Alijah Vera-Tucker. That thins the secondary and the interior line, but Miami's lack of a pass rush blunts the line issue, and its offense is poorly built to exploit the corner absence. Miami is missing LB Willie Gay Jr. and DE Robert Beal Jr., which further weakens a front that already can't get home, and RB Jaylen Wright is questionable in a minor role.

waysToWin.title: Maye picks apart a pass defense
waysToWin.body: Miami allows the most EPA per dropback in the league and barely pressures anyone. That removes New England's biggest current vulnerability: a patched-up interior line in front of a quarterback who holds the ball. Clean pockets should let Maye keep extending his four-week run of efficient passing.

waysToWin.title: Feed Henry and the backs underneath
waysToWin.body: Miami's defense has been gashed by tight ends (worst EPA per play allowed to TE1) and lead backs (RB1s score well over their usual output). Hunter Henry and Rhamondre Stevenson are two of the Patriots' top three targets. That is a natural way to stay ahead of the chains without relying on the stalled run game.

waysToWin.title: Extend drives on third down
waysToWin.body: Miami allows conversions on over half of third downs, 31th in the league. Combined with Vrabel's willingness to go on fourth down, the Patriots can turn possessions into long, clock-eating drives. That keeps Willis and a run-first offense from playing their preferred game.

waysToLose.title: Turnovers keep Miami in it
waysToLose.body: Miami's offense ranks 26th in EPA and can't easily drive the field. The cleanest way for a 1-5 team to win is short fields. New England's giveaway rate is second-worst in the league, and two or three turnovers would turn a mismatch into a coin flip.

waysToLose.title: Miami grinds it on the ground
waysToLose.body: Miami's line leads the league in yards before contact and its offense runs far more than expected. New England is 25th in rushing yards allowed per game. If Willis and the run game stay on schedule, they shorten the game and limit Maye's possessions.

waysToLose.title: Explosives against a thinned secondary
waysToLose.body: Without Davis, a defense already 23rd in explosive pass rate allowed and deep-pass EPA could hand Miami the chunk plays its offense can't manufacture otherwise. One or two broken coverages are how an inefficient offense steals points.

nextGame.watch: Whether New England wins the turnover battle. Everything else in this matchup favors it, and giveaways are the one thing that has repeatedly kept this offense from turning yards into points.

restOfSeason.body:
The passing offense is real and should stay top-ten: it has a track record from 2025 and has been consistently positive for a month. The turnover margin is the most likely thing to improve, since -1 per game is extreme and last year's team was on the positive side. Even modest regression there should lift scoring toward what the yardage implies. What won't fix itself is the run game. The secondary and interior line are also thinner than they were a month ago, with Vera-Tucker not due back until late November.

The schedule is the real test. Miami twice, the Chargers and the Jets are winnable. But the stretch of Buffalo, Minnesota, Kansas City and Denver, plus trips to Detroit and the Packers at home, will decide whether this is a division-title chaser or a wild-card hopeful. A reasonable expectation is a split of the hard games and a sweep of the soft ones, landing around ten wins.
swingFactors: Carlton Davis III's return to the secondary

confidence.note: Seven games, a stable QB and a clear identity, but injuries and a back-loaded schedule add uncertainty.
